papers.title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
papers.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

papers.title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
papers.abstract: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.

papers.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.

papers.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.

papers.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.

papers.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference. We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference. In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.

papers.title: Does the Agent's Map Match the Territory? Architectural Claims in AI Agent Context Files and Their Fit with the Code
papers.abstract: AI coding agents start every session without memory of how a system is built. Developers fill this gap with context files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Agents treat these files as true, so it matters whether they match the code. We study two kinds of architectural claims that can be checked against a repository: path claims, which name folders and files, and dependency rules, which say what may import what. We check 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 context files in 3,346 open-source projects against the code and its history. About 5% of path claims point to paths we cannot find, but we estimate that only 2.2% are real errors, similar to READMEs (3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules behave differently: 33 of 184 (18%) were confirmed broken on the day they were written, usually by older code, and nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: their rules often describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. In an exploratory comparison of 7,480 commits, new rule breaks were rare. Agent-assisted commits broke rules about 1.8 times as often as other commits (0.29% vs. 0.16%), but with only 14 breaks this is not significant: an early signal, not evidence of a difference or of its absence. We used an LLM with human review at each step, and discuss what this offers and risks for mining studies.

papers.title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
papers.abstract: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

topic.title: Similarity-Constrained Reweighting for Complex Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
topic.abstract: Machine learning models for Complex Query Answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs estimate the likelihood of answers that are not reachable via direct traversal. Recent work has proposed extending such queries with soft entity constraints, which require the target variable to be similar or dissimilar to specified sets of entities. We study a more general formulation where similarity constraints are specified on an arbitrary variable in a query, and introduce SCORE: a computationally efficient and interpretable method for incorporating similarity constraints on an arbitrary variable of a query. SCORE is based on a lightweight and interpretable score adjustment function that only requires tuning two hyperparameters on a validation set. Our experiments show that SCORE effectively incorporates preferences while maintaining strong query answering performance. It significantly improves ranking quality when constraints apply to the target variable and performs effectively in the more general case involving constraints on intermediate variables, and its performance remains robust when applied to several existing methods for CQA. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/dfdazac/score.

topic.title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
topic.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.

topic.title: PestWeave: Linking Semantic Modeling and Evidence-Guided Text Modulation through Visual Prototypes for Fine-Grained Pest Learning
topic.abstract: Agricultural pests threaten crop yield and quality, making accurate pest recognition essential for targeted management and sustainable agriculture. Their diverse appearances complicate recognition and motivate multimodal approaches incorporating complementary species knowledge from text. However, complex backgrounds can obscure discriminative visual cues, while textual descriptions may contain information unsupported by the current image, limiting effective cross-modal fusion. To address these challenges, we propose PestWeave, a multimodal framework connecting content-adaptive visual organization with text fusion through visual prototypes. Its visual pathway augments a Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV) architecture with semantic token grouping and three types of auxiliary tokens, enabling content-adaptive scanning and contextual modeling while preserving spatial structure. Feature-similar tokens are reordered into adjacent scanning positions, while cluster prototype, global, and register tokens provide group-level summaries, global context, and additional interaction capacity, respectively. These prototypes also guide text modulation by assessing visual support for semantic components and regulating their relative contributions and overall fusion strength, reducing interference from unsupported descriptions. Extensive experiments on multiple pest recognition datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of PestWeave and its potential for practical pest management.

topic.title: Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields with Bidirectional Diffusion Encoders for Zero-Training Cross-Ontology Medical Coding
topic.abstract: Healthcare systems continually revise clinical taxonomies, update reimbursement schedules, and harmonize cross-border registries. Existing automated coding models bind clinical text understanding to fixed vocabulary-specific heads, requiring manual relabeling and retraining whenever code sets change. We introduce Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields (OCSF), a vocabulary-free framework that decouples clinical document reading from target ontology indexing so one trained encoder can switch across arbitrary medical vocabularies in seconds without target training. A single-pass bidirectional diffusion-pretrained encoder and vocabulary-free decoder map each clinical note into a fixed-dimension two-dimensional state matrix with zero code-specific parameters. Any target ontology is compiled offline on CPU from public text descriptions into a scale-invariant Tikhonov deconvolution operator that suppresses sibling-code interference while preserving source decision thresholds. Trained solely on English MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharge summaries and evaluated without target tuning across 58,706 held-out test notes and five unseen ontologies spanning English ICD-10, MS-DRG, Spanish, Greek, and Chinese (115-185,458 codes), OCSF reaches 63.15% Micro-F1 on in-domain ICD-9 (outperforming a matched closed-vocabulary classifier and eliminating late-epoch tail overfitting) and transfers directly to 26,085 English ICD-10 codes (29.23% recall at gold cardinality), MS-DRG groups, and multilingual terminologies, compiling up to 185,458 codes in under 10 seconds on CPU with sub-millisecond GPU readout.

topic.title: Cache the Knowledge, Not Just the Prompt: Dynamic Datalog as the Action Language for LLM Agents
topic.abstract: An LLM agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph writes a program per question, and its tools evaluate each from scratch. We give the agent a Datalog REPL, a session over a dynamic Datalog engine, in which rules are inserted and retracted like facts while derived facts stay current. Prompt caching reuses the model's processing of what a session shares, and the Datalog REPL reuses the evaluation of it. On chains of questions over three knowledge graphs, agents reuse a relation that the REPL keeps in 179 of 180 cases, with two models, and write fewer output tokens: SQL and Python agents write 23 to 82% more. With SQL tables or a Python namespace, Claude Haiku 5.5 stores almost nothing for later questions, and a chain of seven questions at 13 million facts takes it a median of 48 and 56 s, against 31 s with the REPL. Claude Opus 5.5 matches the REPL by storing tables in SQL, and when the data changes it stores views, which are evaluated again at every read. A relation that the REPL keeps is read like a table and stays current like a view. Datalog is a niche language beside SQL and Python, and with thinking enabled the models answer as accurately with it.

topic.title: Semantic Communication via Federated Learning with Knowledge-Enhanced Networks and Privacy
topic.abstract: This paper presents a novel privacy-preserving semantic communication framework that combines Federated Learning (FL) with Knowledge-Enhanced Networks (KE-NET) for distributed wireless systems. Unlike centralized semantic communication approaches that require data aggregation, our method enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a knowledge-enhanced model while keeping their data and knowledge graphs private. We develop a multi-objective federated optimization strategy that balances semantic fidelity, knowledge integration, channel robustness, and reconstruction accuracy. Theoretical analysis reveals that federated aggregation improves effective SNR for $N$ clients through noise averaging. Numerical results with AWGN and Rayleigh fading channels demonstrate that multi-client federated learning consistently outperforms both single-client and centralized baselines across all SNR conditions, with particularly significant gains in low-SNR scenarios.

topic.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
topic.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.

topic.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
topic.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.
